query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a triple‐pass remelting strategy during SLM processing of high-entropy alloys will refine the microstructure, reduce porosity and fabrication‐induced defects, and thereby improve both the dimensional precision and mechanical integrity of the as-built components.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured high-entropy alloy components fabricated via standard single-pass SLM that exhibit relatively coarse dendritic or cellular structures, residual porosity, and dimensional inaccuracies.
generation.intervention: Apply a triple-pass remelting process—where each deposited layer is re-melted two additional times immediately after deposition—to enhance thermal homogenization and promote complete fusion.
generation.conditions: SLM processing under an inert atmosphere using controlled laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, and layer thickness (e.g., similar to parameters reported in studies on NbMoTaW alloys) in refractory high-entropy alloy systems.
generation.structural_mediator: A more refined and homogeneous microstructure featuring reduced dendrite arm spacing and minimal porosity.
generation.mechanism: Sequential remelting passes promote extended melt pool interaction and thermal homogenization. This leads to finer solidification, minimizes microstructural anomalies, and heals incomplete fusion, thereby reducing dimensional distortions and internal defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline single-pass SLM process, the triple-pass remelted components will exhibit improved dimensional accuracy, higher microhardness and strength, and a significantly reduced porosity level.
generation.baseline: Components fabricated by conventional single-pass remelting SLM methods that typically show higher residual porosity, larger microstructural features, and greater dimensional variability.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected under similar laser energy densities and material systems; the improvement magnitude may vary with alloy composition and inherent thermal properties, and may be limited if excessive thermal input leads to other defects such as cracking.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal number of remelting passes and precise laser parameter settings need further optimization; additionally, effects on ductility and residual stress distribution remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture two sets of high-entropy alloy samples using SLM: one set with the conventional single-pass remelting process and one set using a triple-pass remelting strategy. All other SLM parameters (laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, layer thickness) should be identical. Evaluate the dimensional accuracy, microstructure, and mechanical properties of both sample sets.
measurements: Dimensional accuracy (using coordinate measuring machines or laser scanning)
Porosity analysis (via micro-CT scanning or metallographic image analysis)
Microstructural evaluation (via SEM/EBSD to assess grain size and fusion quality)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples produced with the triple-pass remelting strategy do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision, reduced porosity, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to the single-pass baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using pre-alloyed spherical powder (average diameter 27.2 µm); laser power 90 W, scan speed 600 mm/s, hatch space 80 µm, layer thickness 25 µm, volumetric energy density 75 J/mm³, 180° rotation scanning pattern, high-purity Ar atmosphere.. Test conditions: Compression tests at 25, 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 °C; initial strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; engineering strain limit 0.4; specimens preheated at 10 °C/min; MoS₂ lubricant used.. Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.. Test conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s)..
